children: India’s primary market is heading into one of its busiest stretches of the year, with nearly 25 companies looking to tap investors in September. While the imminent expiry of several Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) approvals is accelerating the pipeline, the rush also reflects improving market sentiment and the depth of domestic liquidity. With 35 of 161 companies holding valid IPO approvals facing an expiry deadline on September 30, issuers are under pressure to bring their offerings to market rather than restart the regulatory process.

In an exclusive interview with BW Businessworld, Vaqarjaved Khan, Senior Fundamental Analyst at Angel One, discusses what is driving the September IPO rush, why strong domestic liquidity is changing the pricing dynamics, and how investors should distinguish fundamentally sound businesses from crowded offerings. He also explains why multiple large issues could test investor appetite and why domestic institutions are increasingly emerging as an important anchor for IPO valuations.
Edited excerpts:
Why has September emerged as one of the busiest IPO months in recent years, and how much is the rush driven by expiring Sebi approvals?

The calendar is doing a lot of the work here. SEBI granted a one-time extension to companies whose approvals fell due between April and September, and that window shuts on 30 September. Of 161 companies holding valid approvals, 35 lapse on that date. Refiling means fresh documents, updated financials and months of delay, so bankers are compressing launches into a few weeks. That said, deadlines only explain the timing. Issuers are also moving because domestic liquidity is deep and sentiment has improved after a cautious first half.
With nearly 25 IPOs competing for investor capital, how should investors separate fundamentally strong issuers from crowded offerings?

Start with the use of proceeds. An issue that is largely an offer for sale tells you promoters are monetising, not funding growth. Then look at whether earnings are consistent over three or four years rather than one polished pre-IPO year. Check the anchor book. Quality mutual funds taking meaningful positions is a real screen, since fund houses anchored only about a quarter of mainboard issues last year. Read the risk factors and related-party disclosures properly. Subscription multiples and grey market premium tell you about demand, not about the business.
Could multiple large IPOs hitting the market together pressure subscription levels, pricing power or liquidity in the secondary market?

Yes, and that is healthy. When 25 issues chase the same rupee, capital rotates to the better ones and marginal offerings struggle to fill their books. Retail applications get spread thin, HNI funding turns selective and QIB attention concentrates. In the secondary market you typically see some churn as investors sell existing holdings to fund applications, though with domestic flows this strong the effect is usually short-lived. Crowding is a discipline mechanism. It forces issuers to price sensibly rather than opportunistically.
Are issuers becoming more realistic on valuations amid heightened investor scrutiny, or does strong domestic liquidity still give them pricing power?

Both are true, in different parts of the market. FY26 saw 366 issues raise roughly Rs. 1.9 lakh crore, but listing gains and oversubscription cooled from the previous year. That is the market repricing risk. Where issuers have visible earnings and a credible anchor book, liquidity still lets them price at the upper band and get away with it. Where the story is thin, books are being scaled back or deals deferred. Pricing power is now earned rather than assumed, which is a meaningful shift from two years ago.
What does sustained mutual fund participation in IPOs tell us about the depth and maturity of India’s domestic capital markets?

It tells us the market no longer depends on foreign flows for price discovery. Mutual funds have committed close to Rs 13,000 crore to 2026 IPOs, and importantly, several continue holding after the anchor lock-in expires rather than selling into listing pops. That behaviour reflects conviction, not allocation-chasing. With SIP flows at record levels, fund managers have durable capital to deploy and can afford to say no. Domestic institutions are now the valuation anchor in most issues. That is genuine market maturity, built on household savings rather than sentiment.
After weaker listing gains despite strong subscription levels in recent years, are investors becoming more valuation-conscious?

Clearly yes. The gap between subscription multiples and listing performance has been the most instructive data point of the last two years. Heavily oversubscribed issues have opened flat or below the offer price, and investors have internalised that oversubscription reflects leverage and allotment mathematics, not value. Sebi's own work showed a majority of allotted shares being sold within a week, which tells you how much of the demand was never long-term to begin with. The result is a market that now reads the offer document rather than the grey market.
Are current IPO valuations adequately supported by earnings growth, or are some issuers already pricing in overly optimistic future growth?

It varies sharply by segment. Established businesses with steady cash flows are largely coming at defensible multiples. The stretch is visible in newer, asset-light and platform businesses, where pricing rests on projected growth several years out and any execution slip leaves no cushion. My test is simple. Compare the implied multiple against listed peers, then ask what growth rate justifies it and whether the company has ever delivered that rate. If the answer relies entirely on the future, the margin of safety sits with the seller, not you.
Beyond listing gains, what should long-term investors evaluate before subscribing to an IPO, and which metrics matter most?

Treat an IPO as a business purchase, not an event. I look at return on capital employed and whether it holds after the fresh issue dilutes the base, operating cash flow against reported profit, debt levels and how the proceeds change them, and promoter holding after the offer. Then valuation relative to listed peers on earnings, not on revenue multiples. Beyond numbers, examine governance, auditor history, related-party transactions and the depth of the management team. Also note the anchor lock-in expiry dates. That supply is predictable and often ignored.
